About the role

The 30-second version: We're hiring a senior platform engineer to be the third senior on our Platform team. You'd own one of three near-term tracks (multi-region control plane, bare-metal capacity, or internal developer platform), take part in a real on-call rotation, and help shape platform decisions across the engineering org. Fully remote, US-only, $175K–$225K, no whiteboard interviews.

Cellular runs a cellular-network connectivity platform that lets device makers, fleet operators, and IoT product teams ship hardware without ever talking to a carrier. Customers hit our API; we handle SIM provisioning, eSIM swaps, multi-carrier routing, billing reconciliation across 184 countries, and the slightly cursed telecom protocols underneath. We're at the point where the platform underneath the API needs a dedicated team — and that's the team you'd help build.

You'll join our Platform group (currently 5 engineers, growing to 9 this year) as the third senior on the team. We own the runtime that every product service deploys onto: a Kubernetes-on-bare-metal fleet across four colocation sites plus two cloud regions, our internal developer platform (a thin Backstage fork), the observability stack (OpenTelemetry → Mimir → Grafana), and the build/CI tooling. We try very hard to be a team that ships paved roads, not gates.

In your first six months we'd hope to see you take primary ownership of one of three tracks: (1) the multi-cluster control plane work that lets product teams deploy a service to all six regions with one PR, (2) the cost-and-capacity rework on our bare-metal pool which currently runs about 60% utilized and could be 85% without drama, or (3) the developer-experience push that takes a service from "scaffolded" to "in production with on-call" in under a day. You'd pick — we're hiring for the senior, not for a pre-decided slot.

We're a fully-remote team with a strong written culture. Most decisions happen in RFCs and async threads with a 48-hour window for input. We do twice-weekly platform sync calls (45 min each), and one all-hands per month. You won't be expected to be online outside of a 4-hour overlap with US Eastern, but you also won't be paged off-hours unless you're on the on-call rotation, which is a real rotation (one week every six) with real handoffs and real comp.

Success in this role looks like: in 90 days you've shipped a meaningful improvement to one platform surface and your team trusts your judgment on architectural calls; in six months product teams are coming to you for platform input early instead of late; in a year, the platform supports two new product surfaces that didn't exist when you joined.

What you'll do

  • Own the design and implementation of one of three near-term platform tracks: multi-region control plane, bare-metal capacity planning, or internal developer platform.
  • Write RFCs, review RFCs, and push back on architectures that won't survive the next 18 months of growth.
  • Operate the platform: triage incidents, run blameless postmortems, and ship the followup work that makes the next incident smaller or impossible.
  • Pair with product engineers on the awkward boundary problems (deploy strategy, blue/green for stateful services, the cost of a new dependency).
  • Contribute to our internal developer platform — a small Backstage fork that today does service scaffolding, docs, and ownership; next year does environment provisioning and budget tracking.
  • Take part in the on-call rotation (one week in six). On-call is paid: $1,500 flat per week plus 1.5× hourly for any pages handled outside business hours.
  • Mentor at least one mid-level engineer on the team — code review, RFC review, and the occasional career conversation.
  • Help us hire: phone screens, take-home reviews (yes, paid — see "red flags" below), and onsite-style pairing interviews.
  • Represent platform in product planning. Catch the "oh wait we need a new region by Q3" stuff before it becomes Q3 instead of as it becomes Q3.
  • Push back on any change to our incident process that erodes the blameless culture. It is hard to get and easy to lose.

What we're looking for

Required Must have

  • 6+ years building and operating production infrastructure at scale — at least two of those years on a platform/SRE/infra team.
  • Deep working knowledge of Kubernetes — not just "I've deployed to it," but "I've debugged a CNI issue at 2am and written the runbook."
  • Strong Go or strong Python (or both). You'll write a lot of controllers, operators, and internal CLIs.
  • Comfort with Infrastructure-as-Code at the scale of "this Terraform repo runs the company" (we use Terraform + Pulumi for different layers).
  • Real experience with observability — instrumenting code, designing dashboards, alerting that humans actually wake up for.
  • Strong written communication. We will read a lot of your writing during the interview.

Preferred Nice to have

  • Experience running Kubernetes on bare metal (we use Talos and Cilium).
  • Built or significantly contributed to an internal developer platform.
  • Familiarity with eBPF, especially in a networking or observability context.
  • Telecom or networking background — eSIM, RADIUS, BGP, anything cursed.
  • Public writing or speaking on infrastructure topics (linking a blog post is nice, not required).
  • Experience hiring and growing a small platform team.

Our stack

Kubernetes (Talos) Cilium / eBPF Go Python Rust (selectively) Terraform Pulumi Postgres 16 ClickHouse NATS OpenTelemetry Grafana Mimir Loki Tempo Backstage (forked) GitHub Actions 1Password Secrets Datadog (legacy, sunsetting)

How to apply

Send a CV (PDF) and a short note — three or four paragraphs is great — to jobs@cellular.example with subject "Senior Platform Engineer — your name". We read everything that comes in. No cover letter template, no recruiter middlemen.

In your note, please tell us about one platform problem you owned end-to-end: what it was, what you tried, what worked, what you'd do differently. We care about how you think, not how polished the writing is.

We aim to make a decision within two weeks of application. Faster if we can. We will never ghost you — every applicant gets a real reply.

What to expect from the process

  1. Stage 1 · 30 min

    Intro call

    With our Platform Lead. Two-way conversation about the role, the team, what you're looking for. Not a screening trap.

  2. Stage 2 · 90 min

    Technical conversation

    Walk through a recent system you built, then design a small piece of platform together on a shared doc. No whiteboard algorithms.

  3. Stage 3 · 4 hours · paid

    Take-home (paid)

    A real platform problem from our backlog. $400 flat, regardless of outcome. Up to 4 hours; we want to see your taste, not your endurance.

  4. Stage 4 · 2 hours

    Team conversations

    Two 45-minute calls with people you'd work with daily. Plus a 30-minute "values and judgment" call with our CTO.

After Stage 4, we make a decision within five business days and provide a written offer with the full compensation rubric attached.

Apply by email Or apply via form →

Red flags we promise we don't have

These are the things we've seen elsewhere that we explicitly don't do. If we ever do any of them, please write to our editorial team and we'll pull the listing.

  • No unpaid take-home exercises. The Stage 3 exercise pays $400 whether we hire you or not.
  • No whiteboard algorithm interviews. We will not ask you to reverse a binary tree on a shared screen.
  • No panel-grilling. The most people in any single interview is two, and the second person is there to take notes.
  • No surprise relocation clause. Remote means remote. There is no office you'd be expected to drift toward.
  • No "we'll get back to you" silence. Every applicant gets a real reply within two weeks of their last interaction.
  • No salary-band coyness. The number in the listing is the band, and the offer lands inside the band based on a published rubric.
  • No 60-hour weeks dressed up as "high agency." Average week is 40–45 hours. On-call is real and comped.
  • No "culture fit" vibes-based rejections. If we say no, we tell you what was missing in writing.

How compensation actually works here

We publish a rubric. The rubric is shared with you in writing before the offer call. The number in the listing — $175K to $225K USD base — is the band for this role and this level. The offer lands inside the band based on the rubric, which weighs three things:

  • Scope demonstrated in interview — what you've actually owned, end-to-end, vs. contributed to. Reviewed against rubric examples for senior platform IC.
  • Adjacent breadth — strong-secondary skills (security, data platforms, ML infra) that increase the platform problems we'd want you on.
  • Mentorship track record — how much you've actually grown the engineers around you, evidenced by specifics in the technical conversation.

We do not negotiate on base. We do not "match" competing offers. If the offer feels low to you, we'd rather hear that and have the conversation about whether we got the rubric scoring wrong, than enter a back-and-forth. Equity grants are slotted in three tiers (0.05% / 0.08% / 0.12%) based on the same rubric.

The team you'd join

You'd report to Dani Park, Platform Lead. Dani has been at Cellular since employee 11, came from Stripe before that, and runs a quiet, written-first team. You'd work most closely with two other senior ICs (Ronan Walsh, focused on the multi-region control plane; Priya Anand, focused on cost & capacity) and two mid-level engineers who joined this year.

Beyond Platform, your closest interfaces are with the SRE team (4 people, in a sister org under the CTO), the Networking team (the actual telecom protocol layer — this is its own kind of cursed and they're great), and the Product Infra team (who own customer-facing API surfaces). Cellular runs a relatively flat eng org — there are 32 engineers under one VPE, organized into 7 small teams.
